VERSAILLES. Monday. May 10, 1873.
The National Assembly met this afternoon.
The Right Center presented an Interpolation,
asking for thoroughly conservative Cabinet. and
demanding explanations from the Government of
the recent changes IN the Ministry. The Assembly
voted that debate on the Interpolation be opened
tomorrow.


NJ. Dufaure, Minister of Justice, submitted con
stitutional bills organizing the public powers and
providing for the establishment of q second
Chamber.


Two test votes were taken during the sitting,
which show that parties in the Chamber are evenly
balanced. The Conservatives are well disciplined,
resolute and fully prepared for the issue Cabinet
and Constitutional questions.


A motion made by the Extreme Left fer the disso-
luton of the Assembly was voted down by heavy
majority and indefinitely postponed.

poor emigrants IN Castle Garden, who

scarcely begun On one side when II was answered

foreign Steamers all contributed to this powerful
cOncerG. AS the bright dash of flame came darling

rately rescued by the crew in another boat.

shore, when the ice parted. A seaman had
brought plank, which was placed across this
chasm, over which all were safely taken. They
lost all their clothing, several ladies being in

its foremost attraction the innate delight OF

The observers eye, no longer dazzled with
imperial halo, with royal purple and princely

Mr.. Abadie, the owner of the Lytle
creek hydraulic mine, was shot and
killed last night while on his way
home from Cucamongo. He left Gu
camongo between and o'clock and
was seen passing Mr.. Smiths place be-
tween five and six, and was never seen
again alive. Last night about one
o'clock, a messenger came to town and
aroused the town Marshal who left in
few moments accompanied by q
posse. They proceeded to Mr.. Aba
dies house, viewed the body, and as
soon as it was light took the back trail.
About two miles below the mines they
saw where the wagon came into the
road. The trail then went into the
brush, aud after wandering about for
three four miles came back into the
road again at place where a small
wash ran parallel to the road. Here
they saw the marks of two men and
one horse. One party started on the
trail and another went back to the
house. Mr.. Abadie was shot twice, one
ball striking him in the left breast
angling, and after passing through
the heart made its exit from the back;
the other ball took. effect in the right
temple, lodging in the brain. From
all appearances he received no warn
ing, but fell forward in the wagon.
The horses became frightened by the
noise of the shots and ran from the
road, but after recovering from their
scare went back again and took the
road home, arriving about midnight.
The gold watch and purse of the de-
ceased were not disturbed, nor was his
shotgun which was under the seat,
loaded and capped. The deceased was
a peaceable, well-disposed citizen; he
had been engaged in mining for some
nine years and was universally liked
and respected. The cause Of the kill
ing is conjectured to arise from law
suit brought against him last summer
for the possession of the Lytle creek
mines, in which Abadie was success
full. Dark hints and threats have
been made, and this is the culmina-
tiOn of the affair,

special despatcttfrom Des Moines to-day gives

night The train left Council Blufs at i've O'Clock

He instantly reversed the engine and applied the

neer John Rafferty,. and the nremany the former

mounted each o horse and. rode on across the

The Modoc campaign has assumed new
and unexpected phase. Our special de-
spatches from the lava BEDS published to-day,
show that the savages do not consider
mastery inactivity the perfection of mill
tary wisdom, and have broken out
from their Businesses and vigorously
attacked the troops. Not content

actually appeared within rifle range Of
General Gillem's camp, and sent volley of
bullets among the tents Of the soldiers.
Of course they were repulsed, and
the hope is entertained that the cavalry
and the Warm Spring Indians will eventually
succeed in destroying them. There is too
much reason to fear, however, that they will
be able to prolong the struggle for some time
and do an infinite amount of damage. In
the meantime the country round about the
lava beds is in ferment, and citizens are fly
ing for their lives.

text:
Another Cold speil-More Snow and


Rain Coming.


Again we have strong indications of the
approach Of cold spell from the region
north of the lakes For two or three days a
heavy storm of snow and wind has been pass
ing, from west to east, over the southern part
of British America and has just reached the
eastern shores of the Continent, near New
foundland. The great snowfall, telegraphed
from Lake Michigan on Thursday morning,
extended yesterday to Lake Huron and Lake
Ontario, as the weather reports show. Fol-
lowing eastward behind the storm centre, the
moving bank of cold atmosphere has given the
boreal northwesterly winds and zero tempera-
lures to the lakes and the bordering
latest thermometrc readings give fifteen
degrees below zero for the North
west and the thermal gradient thence
to the Allegheny, the Catskill and
the White Mountains is by no means steep,
but hardly perceptible When this cold undu-
lation has reached our seaboard and pre-
cipitated its storm-breeding air into the Gulf
Stream vapor we may look out for the usual
sequel of excessive change and the descending
snow and rain.


The Winter conditions ore, however, now so
firmly established over the United States that
it Is hardly possible we can have the southerly
or equatorial current of air for period long
enough to furnish moisture for such a snow
fall as took place last month. That pleasure
must be reserved, probably, for short time,
until the sun, in his northward swing, nears
the Equator. Meantime the immoderate
changes Of temperature, which are the curse
of our Eastern climates and make some sigh
for the mild and balmy shores of the Pacific
slopes, must be guarded against.

GERMAN TRIUMPH OVER CONQUERED FRANCE
The German Imperial Crown has resolved, ap-
parently, that the French people shall not for
get the humiliations which their country en-
dured in the late war. Eighty-six French
flags captured in battle were solemnly placed
in the garrison church of Potsdam yesterday
for the decoration of the walls of the building.
His Majesty Emperor William, the Empress
Augusta, the Imperial Princes and number
of the most distinguished commanders of the
army were present The scene was completely
national, of o compound of military, religious
and corporate citizen character. The Emperor
addressed the assemblage, and thanked the
army for its heroism, pronouncing, like unto
an infalibist, the eternity of its glory
Whether France will accept the dogma, now
that Napoleon is dead, remains to be seen.

Mrs. GOulette was snow bound three
days and nights in the valley this side
of Thirty Mile Spring. Her teamstcr,
who was moving her to Cherry creek,
while wallowing through the snow,
slipped under the wagon and crushed
both his feet; he afterwards was frozen
and unable to proceed. They camped
and remained three days and nights

this section, with little to eat, and no
fire save what they kindled from
small boxes and pieces Of furniture
from the wagon. Under these trying
circumstances Mrs. Goulette, bestri-
ding horse, made Thirty Mile Spring
after hard struggle, lasting all day
far into the night. All this time the
teamster, with his feet mangled, was
lying, helpless and alone, by the road
side. The few blankets thrown around
him afforded but little protection from
the storm. AS soon as Mrs. Goulette
reported at the Springs, men at once
started QUITO rescue the unfortunate
teamster, who was found still alive
and conveyed to the station.

The lynching Of Tarpey, the murderer Of Mrs.
Nicholson. near Monterey, this afternoon created
great excitement in that city. The mob fastened
rope around Tarpey's neck and compelled him to
stand in the box OF wagon. He was then told he
must say all he wanted to, for his time had come.

lynchers then drove the wagon away and left the
man hanging by his neck to the limb OF a tree his
feet almost touching the ground. The crowd
seized the rope and drew Tarpey up higher.
Several Of the lynchers drew pistols and fired into
the body of the diving man. AT last accounts the
body was hanging and the mob watching the
place.

several hours armed men held possession Of
Mon erey and declared they would take Tarpey
safely TO salinas for trial. The jail guards offered
injured. Tarpeys wife, sister and mother were
near the jail and witnessed the whole affair, and
begged, with prayers and tears, the mob not to
injure him. The leaders promised that Tarpey
should not be hurt. The mob numbered over three
hundred and were heavily armed. Tarpey's rela-
tves live in this city and are well known here.

text:
Well nigh half century ago q newly
married couple settled in one of the western
counties of Pennsylvania. They had what
their neighbors deemed fair capital with
which to begin life-a well-stOcked though
small farm, sound health, good common sense,
and more than average amount of shrewd
intelligence and culture Under all this was
sincere trust in God and a jealous, sensitive
love for each other, neither of which their
neighbors knew much about. American back
woods farmers take pride in covering their
emotions under a hide as tough as that of
their own beeves. They had three or four
children, and night after night, over the
kitchen fire, the problem they set themselves
to answer was, what is the best thing we can do
with them, and for them thequestion asked daily
with such wrenching of heart in myriads Of
homes. and answered so differently. The fear
of God seemed to Jacob and his wife the best
heritage to give them the next best plenty
of money. To give them the first, they began
by hedging the children's lives with a system
of rules, borrowed half from the Jewish laws,
half from the theory of their Sect Strict
morality the keeping Of Sunday as periodi-
cal day of penitence and wretchedness. the
learning under penalty of dark closets and
thrashings of the chief duty of man, therein
was their religion. Life they were shown as
strait and hard path through dark valley
with the terrOrs of Sinai behind, and the
traps and pitfalls of flaming hell on either
side. Even Jacobs wife, Mary, holding her
darlings to her breast, than which no
mothers ever 'ached or throbbed with
more tenderness, had no other sermon
to preach to them. 1t never occurred to her
or her husband that it was into just such
fields of grain as those about them, under just
such towering cedars, that Jesus led his dis
cipes and taught them, by the sunshine and
the rain, the tender mercies of God. The
world grew green around them, faded again
and wrapped itself III snow, year after year;
the river sang its mysterious song to the
woods at their very door; and overhead the
stars that had declared to the patriarchs of
the old world the infinite secrets of Jehovah
blazoned them forth STILL unregarded. Day
unto day uttered speech, and night unto night
showed forth knowledge of Him, but both
farmer and wife were deaf and blind. God
was to be approached only through dog
cared catechism, and fields and river were
worth only so much fish and wheat per year.


The children's salvation being thus provided
for, the next thing to be insured was money.
Husband and wife worked and stinted as
only Scotch Irish farmers family can work
or stint. All produce that was salable went
to the market; the children were reared on
the refuse, the skim-milk, poorest bacon, and
watery potatoes Their clothes were coarse
and patched, their feet bare and chilblained
The house grew barer year by year, the
fathers back more bent, his face harder, but
the balance in bank increased dollar by dol
lar. AS for the plump, bonny Mary she had
long ago joined that sisterhood of lean, yellow
skinned, toothless women who, with dirty calico
dresses and wisps of hair twisted up behind, are
sometimes found in farm-houses like CHASTITY
megrims, or daylight specters of wasted life.
When churning and scrubbing were done she
would sit up until near morning washing and
darning their clothes, that they might look
more ."igenteel' than she, dragging her aching
body to look at them when they slept
praying for them with a fierce longing to have
power to be God himself-to be able to pro-
tect and care for them. The boys had
certain strong animal propensities, and physi-
cal. tendencies which required skill and
knowledge to guide or restrain. One had
morbid imagination; another tendency TO
alcoholic poisoning, against which his diet and
training from infancy should have defended

Yesterday afternoon while the thunder storm
was apparently in It's infancy, terrible catastro.
phe was well nigh occurring on the other side of

from the Schuetzen Park, lie the weehawken
Dock recently completed On this dock ore

The Oil is contained in large tank. 1t is
well remembered how the Oil docks Of the Hunters
Point ferry, when ignted by fire last year, ravaged
the coast of the East River. Such an occurrence
was we'll nigh taking place last evening, when the
lightning flashes struck down unsparingly upon
the Wcehawken Oil Dock and almost rent the
slaves OF the enormous tank contain
ing the oil At the hour mentioned the light
ming struck on the rounded edge OF the tank
the mass was ignited and the waves OF fire
rose over the surface. A workman was fortunately
passing by and saw the flames at work. He rushed
down the hill and summoned the Waterman and
workmen. Ladders were soon placed up against
the tank and men climbed them with blankets IN
their hands, the only proper preventives which
could be used; With these they strove to extin-
guish the oily flames for considerable time,
but in vain. The ships anchored near by were
hauled out into the stream to avoid dangers way:
Water was poured % y OF engnes Du
the whole burning lake of oil with blankets and
cloths Of every description until, after some hours
eXertion and careful management the flames were
subdued The tide was moving strongly down the
river towards the bay Had the burning oil
escaped from the tank ana hooded the vicinity
the destruction that would have ensued can
scarcely be imagined.

street, Hoboken, was also struck by the fluid.
Bricks and mortar were torn from the walls, aud
Rther damage done, but no person was injured.

To-day, where low they sleep in death,
Who once were brave in fight
We bring the roses fragrant breath,

Nor ask our hearts who wore the blue,
Nor who the faded gray,
Since battles sweat of crimson dew,
All hate hath washed away.
Awake once more the martial strain
That fed our souls with trust,
In old heroic days Of pain.


Ere swords had gathered rust
The music will not break their rest,
Whose ordered columns lie,
Grim folded hands on silent breast,
Beneath the sunlit sky.
Give pause to eager life of trade,
An hour let bargains cease;
From Valor's fervent pulse was made
The golden tide Of Peace;
Let manhood's heart and childhood's hand,
And woman's loveliest bloom,
Through all the WIDE untroubled land,
Adorn the soldiers tomb.
All North and South, richer art

For Natures throbbing mother heart
Hath quicker beat than ours;
Her blades of grass, her cloth Of gold,

This Decoration Day.
She spreads as soft her daisied turf
On mounds without name,

Her lingering touch in blossom falls

And yet are Freedoms own.
SO, where to-day they sleep in death,

LAVA BED CAMP, Cal, May II, 1873


Yesterday the scouting party under Captain
Hasbrouck and Donald Mckay met the
Modocs at the head of Sorass Lake. It seems
they had been encamped the night previous,
expecting to meet the Indians in that vicin-
ity, though the only signs seen were fresh
tracks of one mule and pony Twelve men
of Jackson's cavalry were guarding the horses,
when,


IN TEE GRAY OF THE MORNING,
the Modocs attacked the camp. They had
left their horses back some distance and
crept upon the sleepers, the first fire killing
one and wounding eight men. The soldiers
sprang to their arms, and, with the Warm
Springs, in few minutes were driving the
Modocs s~rs 49,


The country was rather open, but still
rough, for two miles, which the Modocs must
pass to reach the lava bed.


THE WARM SPRINGS
ran them so fast that the Modocs lost twenty
one horses and some loads of ammunition. One
Warm Spring was killed. The Indians were
driven all day and last night Donald Mckay
sent back for water, saying he could hold
them. There were


THmTY-FoUR MoDocs IN THE FIGHT
all the band They were working around for
the timbered butte, near the Sand Bluff, where
they hope to escape by way of Pit Range if
forced to leave the lava beds. This is q de-
cisive victory, and will do more to encourage
the soldiers and discourage the Modocs than
all the previous fighting. The Warm Springs
fought nobly and to the purpose.


THE OFFICIAL REPORT,
at half-past seven o'clock this evening, states
that the troops lost two hlled-C Corporal Tot
tenn, Of Troop G, First cavalry, and one Warm
Spring Indian. One Modoc is known to be
killed, and perhaps others.


Tomorrow 10 men from this side are
ordered to move towards the scene Of the con-
hict. General Davis hopes that we now have
them whipped, and will improve the occasion.
General Gillem will not be lnterfered with,
for his policy has been true so far. think
we can see the beginning of the end.

SOUTHWEST PASS, La, Oct. H. 1873.
The ship Tasmania (Br.), Willis, master, forty
eight days from st. Nazare, France, has arrived
here. She experienced a severe hurricane when
between Cape Antonio and Campeachy, during
which she lost two lower topsalls and other sails.
On the 9th inst. she sighted the hull OF vessel,
bearing north, with all her masts gone close TO the
deck, but with spar rigged up forward and aft.
She proved to be the British ship Lady Russell,
from Liverpool for Mobile Her Captain refused
assistance but asked to be reported all well.


On the 7th inst. the Tasmania came across the
British bark Isle OF Skye from Progreso, Mexico for
New York, with her rudder and masts gone and
every sail and rope blown away. The crew had
been three days without water, and were nearly
all disabled and wished to leave the vessel The
Captain OF the Tasmania took them or and brought
them to New Orleans. The Captain and crew fred
the Isle OF Skye before leaving her.

The following special despatch to the
HERALD has been received from our CORE
Spondent at Khiva, by way of London:-


LONDON, August 3, 1873.
The HERALD special correspondent at Khiva
has forwarded the following report from the
Khanate capital, under date of June II, by
way of Orenburg:-


THE RUSSIANS AFTER VICTORY.


Full details of the capture OF Khiva by the
Russian troops have been anticipated by pre-
.vious dispatches General Kaufman is well
satisfied with the result of the campaign.


THE KILLED AND WOUNDED.


The entire Russian loss is twenty-one killed
and ninety-two wounded, including twenty
six casualties incurred among the naval sup
porting force on land by reason of its having
been decoyed into Turkoman camp, where
Two officers and fourteen men were massacred.
SOLDIER scIoNs OF THE IMPERIAL HOUSE.
The Grand Dukes Nicholas and Leuchten-
berg were greatly distinguished in the affair of
The Goth of May. They were under fire
during space of two hours. Both princes
are great favorites with the army.
CAMP sPo1Ls AND TERRITORIAL ACQUISITIONS.
The Russians captured twenty cannons and
large quantity Of munitions of war.
Khiva city is dirty squald town. The
palace of the Khan is shabby. The environs
Of the metropolis are very rich and the coun-
Try delightful. The vegetation in the rural
districts is rapid and fruitful and the product
beautiful.


There is strong pro-Russian party among
The trading community The population is
very quiet and respectful.


SLAVES SET FREE.


Forty thousand slaves were let free by the
eonquerors.


TREATY MAKING AND TERROR.


General Kaufman will remain until the
terms Of the Russo-khivan Treaty are full
illed by the Khan and also in view of
probable contingent necessity which may
present for further service on his part in
marching Russian expedition to chastise the
Turkoman tribes and break down their mill
sary and feudatory power; they having proved
themselves cowardly and treacherous in their
dealings with the Gar and brutal and cruel
toward the Persian slaves.


MARTIAL LAW EXECUTIONS.


Two slave masters have been hanged for
commission of theft and violence.


ALONE AMONG FRIENDS.


The HERALD correspondent is the only
stranger in the Russian camp. He is treated
with great kindness by General Kaufman
and the officers of his command, because Of
yhe sincere friendship which the Russians en-
tertain for Americans.

played havoc with the forces in search of them.
There were sixty-nine men detailed under the

killed and wounded. Sixteen were killed and
thirty-three were wounded.

dians and much absurd verbiage is slung
around on the subject. But we are inclined to
think that the Modocs were not properly treat
ed-they were imposed upon, and were not the
orginators of the troubles. Then the entire
Indian race must not be slaughtered if a few
Modoes did act in bad faith. And for this last
slaughter the Indians are not most to blame.
It could not have occurred without blunder-
ing of some sort

One Man Instantly Killed and Another

Railroads.


While Michel Dupus, aged twenty-one, native
Of Canada, residing at 1872 Third avenue, and
Daniel Geary, aged thirty, unmarried miner,
born in Ireland and residing at 143 East Ninety
second street. were engaged in sinking the tracks
OF the Harlem and New Haven Railroads in Fourth
avenue, between Ninety second and Ninety third
streets, pursuant to recent resolution of
the Common Council, q blast which they were load
ing in the main shaft Of the excavations suddenly
exploded, instantly killing Dupuis and terribly in
juiing Geary, whose left leg was broken, his eye
sight destroyed and his head and body terribly
burned.


Offlcers Of the Twenty. third precinct rendered
prompt assistance, and Police Surgeon White, who
was summoned, attended Geary, who was mme-
diately afterwards renewed to the Reception Hos
pital, in Nnetynlnth street, where he new lies in
a critical condition.


The mangled body Of Dupuis was taken to the
Morgue where Coroner Keenan,, who had been
notified, subsequently held an inquest which
showed the fatal occurrence to have been acci-
dental, but caused by carelessness on the part OF
the deceased and the injured man. The body OF
Dupuis was delivered to friends for transporta-
tion to Canada for lnterment.

which brought about these results; the evil
lies in bad construction, old age and false
ideas of naval architecture.

rived in Panama on the 5th instant, from Costa
Rico, and the revolution which slumbered since
President Nieva was banished has broken out
afresh. The evening following the arrival of
Carreosa she convened injecting, declaring

here for the protection Of foreigners had
been acting traitorously to the General
government as well as the state by interfering
with the late revolt which deposed INieva, and
expressed his intention of disarming and com
pelling them to leave the state on the morrow.

San Jose, by the state troops advancing upon
the national forces. After desperate fighting of

claim that they attacked for safety. At day-
break this morning the firing was reopened
and continued with slight intermission until
one O'Clock, when truce was agreed upon.

has ended satisfactorily, and the trouble is over

former project oHCalon, as the provisional

the damage to which is estimated at $4,000.
Two pleasure yachts one containing fourteen,
the other nine persons, were capsized during the
storm on Lincoln Park. They were, fortunately,
near shore and all were saved To-day was the
hottest OF the season, the thermometer being 90
